sn47.7:2.13: In his note on this Sutta, Bodhi acknowledges the difficult reading _kaṭṭha-kataṅgāre_ and proposes the emendation _kaṭṭha-kaliṅgare_ based on the Buddhist Sanskrit _kāṣṭha-kaḍambara_. He then takes it to mean a block of wood, to which the hunter fastens the monkey before leaving with both monkey and block. This, however, creates several problems. Since both _kaṭṭha_ and _kaliṅgara_ mean “block of wood”, why the compound? Why does the hunter need to secure the monkey to the wood, when the whole point of the simile was that the monkey was stuck? Why read the verb _avassajjetvā_ as “having fastened” when the normal meaning of _avassajati_ is “release”, confirmed by the BJT reading _uddharitvā_, and agreeing with other occurrences of _yena kāmaṁ pakkamati_, which are preceded by someone being released ([mn66:10.1](), [an5.75:14.4](), [an8.14:7.1]())? And why would the hunter carry a log of wood out from such a remote region? I propose that _kaṭṭhakataṅgāra_ is a corrupted form related to the Sanskrit _kāṣṭhakadalī_, the wild plantain; perhaps the *Musa mannii*, a rare species found today in Arunchal Pradesh and sometimes known as the Indian Dwarf Banana. The hunter spears the trapped monkey while it is stuck to its favorite fruit tree, killing it, then pries it off and goes on his way.
